newsitem.title: USA: Senators get administration proposals on Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Senators get administration proposals on Mexico.

text.p: High-level Clinton administration officials on Monday presented a proposal to key senators on how to deal with congressional dissatisfaction over Mexico's handling of drug trafficking.

The officials, led by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, met the three senators for more than an hour in the office of Georgia Republican Paul Coverdell in an apparent effort to head off Senate "decertification" of Mexico as an ally in the anti-drug war.
California Democrat Dianne Feinstein told reporters afterwards: "The administration submitted a draft and there are some concerns about it and we will see if we can work them out overnight."

Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, a Texas Democrat, said there were some good parts in the administration proposal and added, "I'm cautiously optimistic that we might have something that I think might be acceptable."
Coverdell said that he hoped the Senate would act this week on the issue.
At issue is whether the Senate will follow the House last week in voting to "decertify" Mexico -- an action the Mexican government would regard as an attack on its sovereignty.

The three senators and the administration officials, who also included White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger and Retired Gen. Barry McCaffrey, director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, refused to give any details of their meeting.
The senators said staff members would work on the proposal overnight.
Both Feinstein and Coverdell have proposed decertification of Mexico with a waiver of sanctions. Hutchison has countered with a non-binding resolution that would merely express the views of Congress.
Other senators have said that this approach is not sufficient.
Senate Republican leader Trent Lott said earlier on Monday he expected the Senate would debate a resolution this week.

The House last week voted to give Mexico 90 days to improve its performance or face decertification as a reliable ally in the fight against drugs. The Clinton administration strongly opposed the House measure, which is harshly critical of its own anti-drug policies.

"There's a bipartisan effort under way to see what can be agreed to that would make our feelings very clear that we are dissatisfied with the degree of cooperation and the results that we're getting from the so-called war on drugs," Lott said.
He added: "At the same time I think there is a feeling that we don't want to cut off the continuing law enforcement effort and communications ... that might worsen the situation."

Administration officials have warned that if Congress overturns Clinton's Feb. 28 certification of Mexico, President Ernesto Zedillo's progress on controlling drugs would be undermined and investors could lose confidence in Mexico, denting its economic recovery.
